paper_title: Knowing When to Teach: Learning from Teachable Prefixes in Multilingual Reasoning Distillation

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD) improves reasoning by training a student on its own reasoning, using the same model conditioned on reference solutions as a teacher. Applying OPSD to multilingual reasoning requires the teacher to provide useful feedback across languages, even when the student makes mistakes in intermediate steps. We observe a phenomenon we call Teacher Drift: as these mistakes accumulate, the teacher may follow the student's incorrect steps instead of correcting them. Our analysis shows that this shift tends to occur earlier in lower-resource languages. To account for these differences across languages, we propose Teachable On-Policy Self-Distillation (TOPSD), which determines where and whether teacher supervision should be applied to each reasoning trajectory. TOPSD uses teacher-student likelihood to estimate where drift begins and select a prefix for supervision. It then verifies whether the teacher can recover the correct answer from that prefix, applying distillation only to prefixes that pass verification. Experiments on multilingual mathematical reasoning across ten languages and three model scales show that TOPSD consistently outperforms conventional OPSD, particularly in low- and medium-resource languages.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Large language models (LLMs) (Brown et al., 2020; Achiam et al., 2023; Team et al., 2023; Grattafiori et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2024; Guo et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2025) have demonstrated strong reasoning capabilities on complex tasks such as mathematical problem solving, logical inference, and complex question answering. On-Policy Distillation (Ross et al., 2011; Lin et al., 2020; Agarwal et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2026a) further improves these capabilities by training the student with dense token-level supervision on reasoning it generates. Corresponding authors. 1 Figure 1: Teacher Drift in Korean reasoning example. The teachers next-token predictions are evaluated on prefixes of one student trajectory. At = 36 and 180, it predicts 2 instead of the students 0, correcting dodecagons side count from 10 to 12; at = 314, it predicts 0, following the repeated error. English translations are shown in gray. Specifically, the teacher conditions on the students prefix, the sequence of tokens generated so far, and uses its next-token distribution to supervise the student. On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD) (Zhao et al., 2026) uses the same model as both student and teacher, with reference solutions provided only to the teacher. This enables learning from modelgenerated reasoning with dense teacher feedback, without separate heavy teacher model (Shenfeld et al., 2026; Hübotter et al., 2026). However, extending these benefits to multilingual reasoning is challenging due to the limited reasoning capabilities of the teacher model across languages. Since the language model is largely pretrained on high-resource languages such as English, it shows substantially weaker performance in lower-resource languages than in high-resource languages (Zhao et al., 2025). Prior work, such as COPSD (Liu et al., 2026), addresses it by using English reference solutions to draw on the models stronger reasoning ability in English and improve teacher supervision in the target language. While this effort focuses on strengthening the it remains underexplored whether the teacher, teacher can provide reliable supervision throughout the students reasoning. We therefore investigate how the reliability of teacher supervision changes as the students reasoning unfolds across different languages. We observe that the teacher may initially correct the students errors, but begin to follow the students incorrect reasoning as these errors accumulate, even with access to reference solutions. We refer to this shift as Teacher Drift. Figure 1 illustrates this behavior in Korean reasoning example, where the student repeatedly states that regular dodecagon has ten sides. At the first two occurrences, the teacher predicts token that corrects the number to twelve; at later occurrence, it predicts the same incorrect token as the student. Our multilingual analysis further shows that Teacher Drift tends to emerge earlier in lower-resource languages, suggesting that the teachers ability to provide reliable supervision varies across languages. These observations motivate identifying where the teacher can still provide useful supervision within each reasoning trajectory. Based on these observations, we propose Teachable On-Policy Self-Distillation (TOPSD), which determines where teacher supervision remains appropriate and whether it should be applied. TOPSD estimates where Teacher Drift begins to select teachable prefix, and then verifies whether the teacher can recover the correct answer from that prefix. If verification succeeds, distillation is applied to the teachable prefix. Our contributions are summarized as follows: We identify Teacher Drift, where the privileged teacher begins to follow the students incorrect reasoning as errors accumulate, and characterize its language-dependent patterns through likelihood and recovery analyses. We propose TOPSD, which combines trajectory-specific prefix selection with teacher recovery verification to determine where and whether to apply supervision. We demonstrate the effectiveness of TOPSD reasoning for multilingual mathematical across model scales, with improvements particularly in lowand medium-resource languages.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Multilingual Reasoning. Despite advances in LLM reasoning, performance remains uneven across languages, particularly in low-resource settings (Shi et al., 2023; Xuan et al., 2025; Ghosh et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025). Prior work has sought to improve multilingual reasoning through multilingual post-training (Payoungkhamdee et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2024; Lai and Nissim, 2024; Ranaldi and Pucci, 2025; She et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2026b) and cross-lingual reasoning transfer (Huang et al., 2023; Qin et al., 2023; Zhu et al., 2024; Tran et al., 2025; Barua et al., 2026). More recently, COPSD (Liu et al., 2026) extends on-policy self-distillation to multilingual reasoning by leveraging English problems and reference solutions as privileged teacher information. Our work complements these efforts by improving the reliability of multilingual on-policy self-distillation, particularly when errors accumulate in student-generated reasoning. Post-Training for Reasoning. Reasoning capabilities are commonly improved through selftraining, reinforcement learning, and knowledge distillation. Self-training bootstraps from modelgenerated rationales (Zelikman et al., 2022), while recent post-training methods learn from sampled reasoning trajectories using verifiable outcomes, verifiers, or step-level feedback (Shao et al., 2024; Trung et al., 2024; Chu et al., 2025; Hosseini et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024; Hwang et al., 2024; Xu et al., 2025). Within knowledge distillation (Hinton et al., 2014), GKD and related methods supervise student-generated sequences with teacher predictions (Lin et al., 2020; Gu et al., 2024; Agarwal et al., 2024; Ko et al., 2024, 2025), while OPSD uses the same model as student and privileged teacher under different conditioning contexts (Zhao et al., 2026). Recent work further improves the distillation with guided or trust-region rollouts (Li et al., 2026; Plyusov et al., 2026), selective or adaptive token-level supervision (Wang et al., 2026; Jang et al., 2026), and trajectory refinement (Jiang et al., 2026). We characterize language-dependent Teacher Drift and verify Teacher Recoverability before distilling selected prefixes of original student 2 trajectories.

sections.title: 3 Preliminaries
sections.content: On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD) (Zhao et al., 2026) improves reasoning by training student on its own generated trajectories with dense supervision from the same model conditioned on reference solutions, without requiring separate teacher model. Let denote reasoning dataset consisting of set of input problems and their reference solutions y. Rather than relying on separate teacher model, OPSD instantiates both the student and the privileged teacher from the same underlying language model πθ, while conditioning them on different information. The student pS observes only the problem x, whereas the privileged teacher pT additionally observes the reference solution y: pS( x) πθ( x), pT( x, y) πθ( x, y). For each problem x, the student first samples trajectory (1) ˆy = (cid:0)ˆy1, . . . , ˆyˆy (cid:1) pS( x). (2) Then, OPSD trains the student by minimizing the token-level distributional discrepancy between the two policies along the student-generated trajectory: LOPSD = E(x,y) Eˆy pS( x) 1 ˆy ˆy (cid:88) t=1 D(pS,t, pT,t) , (3) where pS,t := pS( x, ˆy<t) and pT,t := pT( x, y, ˆy<t) are the student and teacher next-token distributions conditioned on the same studentgenerated prefix, and D(, ) denotes distributional divergence. The simple way to design teacher prompt in multilingual settings is to use reference solution y(L) for each target language (i.e., y(L)). However, the model may find it harder to make use of reasoning trace written in non-English language, since most of its reasoning ability is learned from English data. So, COPSD (Liu et al., 2026) provides the English question x(EN) and its reference solution y(EN) as the privileged knowledge to leverage the reasoning capabilities of LLMs. The teacher prompt for target language can be written as: (cid:0)x(EN), y(EN)(cid:1). Even though OPSD variants have shown their success in multiple reasoning tasks, it is still underexplored in multilingual settings. This is particularly challenging because OPSD relies on the teacher to provide reliable supervision over studentgenerated trajectories. In multilingual settings, this supervision faces two potential challenges. First, errors in student-generated prefixes may make it difficult for the teacher to provide corrective guidance. Second, the teacher itself may have limited reasoning capabilities in non-English languages, where training data is often less abundant. These challenges raise concerns about whether the teacher can consistently provide reliable supervision throughout student rollouts.

sections.title: 5 Teachable On-Policy Self-Distillation
sections.content: To address limitations of OPSD in multilinguality, such as Teacher Drift and degradation of teacher recoverability, we propose Teachable On-Policy SelfDistillation (TOPSD), which determines where and whether to apply teacher supervision along studentgenerated trajectories. As illustrated in Figure 3, TOPSD consists of two stages: Teachable prefix selection and Teacher Recoverability Verification. Teachable prefix selection uses the cumulative teacher-student likelihood ratio to identify teachable prefix before sustained teacher drift. Teacher recoverability verification then evaluates whether the teacher can recover the correct answer from the selected prefix. Only when verification succeeds does TOPSD apply distillation to the selected states of the original student trajectory to provide the meaningful guidance. 5.1 Teachable Prefix Selection As observed in Section 4.1, Teacher Drift manifests as increasing likelihood alignment between the teacher and student along student-generated trajectories. sections.title: 6 Experiments
sections.content: 6.1 Experimental Settings Dataset and Languages. We use the mulreleased by tilingual OpenThoughts dataset COPSD (Liu et al., 2026), sampling 500 training instances per language (5,000 in total). We consider ten languages: Bengali (BN), English (EN), Spanish (ES), Japanese (JA), Korean (KO), Russian (RU), Swahili (SW), Telugu (TE), Thai (TH), and Chinese (ZH). Models and Baselines. We conduct experiments using Qwen3-1.7B, Qwen3-4B, and Qwen38B (Yang et al., 2025). The student is trained with LoRA (Hu et al., 2022), while the privileged teacher is the frozen base model conditioned on the English problem and reference solution. We compare TOPSD against the base model (Vanilla), OPSD (Zhao et al., 2026), and COPSD (Liu et al., 2026). Training and Evaluation. Following OPSD (Zhao et al., 2026) and COPSD (Liu et al., 2026), we use fixed privileged teacher and fullvocabulary logit distillation. We evaluate multilingual mathematical reasoning on the PolyMath High split (Wang et al., 2025), reporting Avg@3 and Pass@3 across ten languages. Detailed training configurations and evaluation protocols are provided in Appendix A. 6 Overall Performance. Table 1 reports Avg@3 and Pass@3 on PolyMath High across three Qwen3 model scales. TOPSD achieves the best overall performance for both metrics at every scale. For Avg@3, TOPSD reaches 11.60%, 17.79%, and 25.12% with Qwen3-1.7B, 4B, and 8B, improving over the strongest baseline by 1.65, 1.07, and 2.64 percentage points, respectively. The corresponding Pass@3 scores are 18.72%, 26.00%, and 35.28%, with gains of 2.08, 0.88, and 3.36 points. These consistent improvements indicate that selective teacher supervision remains effective as model scale increases. Performance Across Language Resource Levels. The gains are most consistent in lowand mediumresource languages, where TOPSD achieves the best Avg@3 and Pass@3 at all three model scales. Relative to the strongest baseline, Avg@3 improves by 0.89-3.47 percentage points and Pass@3 by 0.80-4.00 points across these groups. The gains are largest for Qwen3-8B in the medium-resource group, improving Avg@3 from 24.09% to 27.56% and Pass@3 from 35.73% to 39.73%. Overall, TOPSD delivers its strongest and most consistent improvements in lowand medium-resource languages while remaining competitive in highresource languages. 6.3 Ablation Studies Is Teachable Prefix Selection Alone Sufficient? We investigate whether Teachable Prefix Selection alone provides reliable supervision or whether Teacher Recoverability Verification is also necessary. Table 2 compares COPSD with three variants that supervise all selected prefixes, only failedrecovery prefixes, or only successful-recovery prefixes (TOPSD). Prefix selection alone improves Avg@3 from 9.95% to 10.76%, while verification further increases it to 11.60%. In contrast, supervising failed-recovery prefixes yields lower performance than supervising all selected prefixes or successful-recovery prefixes, highlighting the importance of verifying teacher recoverability. 6.4 Additional Analysis Teachable Prefix Selection Across Model Scales. To examine whether TOPSD generalizes beyond multilingual settings, we additionally evaluate it on the English mathematical reasoning benchmarks used in the original OPSD study (Zhao et al., 2026). We train Qwen3-4B on 500 English mathematical reasoning problems sampled from OpenThoughts (Guha et al., 2026) for 160 optimization steps and compare Vanilla, OPSD, and TOPSD. We evaluate on AIME 2024 (Zhang and Math-AI, 2024) and AIME 2025 (Zhang and MathAI, 2025), reporting Avg@3 and Pass@3. As shown in Table 4, TOPSD achieves the highest Pass@3 on AIME 2024 and improves both Avg@3 and Pass@3 on AIME 2025. sections.title: 7 Conclusion
sections.content: TOPSD on Bengali mathematical reasoning problem asking for the sum of all integer bases > 9 such that 17b divides 97b. Both models begin from similar correct formulation, expressing the two numbers as + 7 and 9b + 7 and establishing the corresponding divisibility condition. COPSD then repeatedly restates that 9b + 7 must be divisible by + 7, without deriving further constraints on b, and fails to produce formatted final answer. In contrast, TOPSD introduces an integer quotient through 9b + 7 = k(b + 7) and rearranges the equation into (9 k)b = 7(k 1). It then identifies the valid bases = 21 and = 49, corresponding to = 7 and = 8, respectively, and obtains their sum, 70. This example illustrates how the two models diverge after correct initial setup: COPSD becomes trapped in repetition, whereas TOPSD develops the divisibility condition into concrete constraints and completes the solution. We identify Teacher Drift, failure mode in which privileged teacher increasingly follows erroneous student reasoning as errors accumulate in the prefix. To address this, we propose Teachable On-Policy Self-Distillation (TOPSD), which combines Teachable Prefix Selection and Teacher Recoverability Verification to determine when teacher supervision remains appropriate and whether it should be trusted. Experiments on PolyMath High across ten languages and three Qwen3 model scales show that TOPSD consistently outperforms OPSD and COPSD, with particularly strong gains in lowand medium-resource languages. These results demonstrate that reliable on-policy self-distillation requires not only strong teacher, but also knowing when the teacher remains able to teach and whether its guidance should be trusted. Extending this approach beyond mathematical reasoning is promising direction for future work.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: Our findings are limited to mathematical reasoning, and their generalization to other reasoning domains and model families remains to be explored. In multilingual settings, the usefulness of teacher supervision may depend on the models existing capabilities in each language, so the extent of improvement may vary across languages and models. Our current setup also uses English reference solutions as privileged information, leaving other source languages and settings without such resources unexplored. Future work could investigate how the language and quality of reference solutions affect supervision and evaluate the approach across broader range of multilingual reasoning tasks.

sections.title: Ethical Considerations
sections.content: AI assistance. AI tools were used to assist with drafting and revising the manuscript. The authors retain responsibility for all content, results, and claims. Potential risks. TOPSD improves multilingual mathematical reasoning, while performance differences across languages remain. Models trained with TOPSD may inherit biases and errors from their underlying models and training data, which can affect the quality of assistance available to speakers of underrepresented languages. We report results for individual languages and resource groups to make these differences visible. Applications should be evaluated in their intended languages and contexts, with attention to whether aggregate improvements translate into benefits for the users they serve. Training and teacher verification also consume computational resources and have associated environmental costs. We document our training configurations and hardware to support reproducibility and assessment of computational requirements. These costs should be considered alongside performance gains when scaling the approach to additional models and languages.

sections.title: A Additional Experimental Details
sections.content: Hyperparameter Value Training Details. We use Qwen3-1.7B, Qwen34B, and Qwen3-8B as the underlying models for both the student and the privileged teacher (Yang et al., 2025). The student is trained with LoRA (Hu et al., 2022), while the privileged teacher is obtained by disabling the LoRA adapters and freezing the underlying base model. Following the COPSD (Liu et al., 2026) configuration, we use LoRA with rank of 64 and scaling factor of 128. The adapters are applied to all attention and MLP projection layers in each Transformer block, including q_proj, k_proj, v_proj, o_proj, gate_proj, up_proj, and down_proj. We do not apply LoRA to the token embeddings, language-model head, or normalization layers. For each training instance, we sample one onpolicy trajectory from the student with maximum completion length of 2,048 tokens and sampling temperature of 1.1. We train only the LoRA parameters for 160 optimization steps using AdamW (Loshchilov and Hutter, 2019) with bfloat16 precision, learning rate of 1 106, gradient clipping of 0.1, and an effective prompt batch size of 32. TOPSD performs full-vocabulary logit distillation using the fixed privileged teacher. Unless otherwise specified, TOPSD uses likelihood-ratio threshold of τ = 0.9 and persistence length of = 4. For Teacher Recoverability Verification, the privileged teacher greedily generates continuation from the selected prefix. Its continuation is evaluated using rule-based verifier that extracts the final answer from boxed{} and compares it with the ground-truth answer. Only trajectories that pass verification contribute to distillation, with the loss averaged over supervised tokens per trajectory and balanced equally across active languages. Implementation Details. All experiments are conducted using either four NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPUs or four NVIDIA H200 GPUs. For Teacher Recoverability Verification, the privileged teacher greedily generates continuation from the selected student prefix, with maximum continuation length of 8,192 tokens for Qwen3-1.7B and Qwen34B and 12,288 tokens for Qwen3-8B. We evaluate the resulting trajectory using rule-based verifier that extracts the final answer from boxed{} and compares it with the ground-truth answer. sections.title: C Additional Multilingual Results
sections.content: Comparison with Fixed-Prefix Truncation. To investigate whether the improvements of TOPSD arise simply from restricting distillation to shorter prefixes, we compare our adaptive prefix selection with fixed-prefix baseline. Specifically, the fixedprefix baseline retains the first 10% of each studentgenerated trajectory for distillation, regardless of the estimated drift point. We choose 10% based on the average relative cutoff position of 10.47% observed with Qwen3-1.7B under our default configuration (K = 4, τ = 0.9), as reported in Tables 3 and 8. Both methods use the same Teacher Recoverability Verification procedure and training configuration, differing only in their prefix selection strategies. As shown in Table 7, TOPSD outperforms fixed-prefix truncation, suggesting that its improvements cannot be explained solely by restricting supervision to early reasoning states. Instead, adaptively selecting teachable prefixes across languages and individual student trajectories provides additional benefits over fixed cutoff. Sensitivity to K. Table 8 examines how the persistence length affects cutoff selection and downstream performance, with other hyperparameters fixed. The cutoff detection rate measures the proportion of trajectories with detected cutoff, while the relative cutoff position denotes the cutoff location normalized by trajectory length. As increases, the detection rate decreases slightly, while cutoffs tend to occur later. This reflects the stricter persistence requirement, which retains longer prefixes for potential supervision. Avg@3 increases from = 1 to = 4 but declines at = 8, with the default setting (K = 4) achieving the highest score of 11.60% among the evaluated values.

sections.title: D Additional Qualitative Analysis
sections.content: Qualitative Comparison of Reasoning Trajectories Figures 5, 7, and 8 compare the reasoning trajectories produced by the Qwen3-1.7B vanilla model, COPSD, and TOPSD on three multilingual mathematical reasoning problems spanning high-, medium-, and low-resource languages. Rather than considering only final-answer correctness, we highlight the local reasoning error that determines each solution. In the high-resource Spanish example, both the base model and COPSD omit the cross-term 3a2 1 when matching the coefficient of x2017, whereas TOPSD correctly uses 3a2 1 + 3a2 = 19. In the medium-resource Thai example, the base model uses an incorrect parameter range and COPSD reports only an incomplete set of solutions, while TOPSD factorizes the equation and counts both solution families over their full symmetric ranges. In the low-resource Telugu example, the base model forms an incorrect triangle-area expression and COPSD produces repetitive reasoning without valid derivation, whereas TOPSD derives the correct determinant-based area and obtains the limiting value. Across all three examples, the improvement from TOPSD is not limited to changing the final answer. TOPSD corrects the key intermediate derivation on which the remainder of the solution depends, resulting in more coherent and complete 14 Figure 5: Qualitative comparison on high-resource Spanish problem. Both the base model and COPSD omit the cross-term 3a2 1 and incorrectly use 3a2 = 19, producing the answer 22. TOPSD correctly matches the coefficient using 3a2 1 + 3a2 = 19 and obtains the correct answer 352. English translations are shown in gray. reasoning trajectories across language-resource levels. Additional Examples of Teacher Drift. While Figure 1 of the main paper directly examines the teachers next-token predictions at distillation states, Figure 6 provides complementary completion-based view. We greedily continue the same privileged teacher independently from progressively longer prefixes of single Swahili student trajectory. The recurrence implies 2 1 = 3, 3 1 = 9, 41 = 27, and 51 = 81, giving the correct answer 81 3 = 78. However, the student incorrectly substitutes 4 1 = 3 into 5 1 = 3 (4 1), obtaining 51 = 9 and the wrong answer 93 = 6. The red highlights mark this incorrect substitution and its propagation, which reappears later in the students reasoning. At = 600 and = 700, the teacher recovers despite the earlier error already being present in the prefix. It correctly computes 4 1 = 27 and uses this value to obtain 5 1 = 81, as highlighted in blue, ultimately returning 78. At = 768, the teacher instead continues the incorrect derivation and returns 6, matching the students wrong answer. Thus, in this trajectory, the teacher can initially recover from an erroneous prefix but fails to do so after the prefix is extended with further incorrect reasoning. Figure 6: Completion-based illustration of Teacher Drift. The same privileged teacher is greedily continued from three progressively longer prefixes of single student completion. It recovers the correct answer 78 at = 600 and = 700, but follows the students incorrect reasoning and returns 6 at = 768. This provides an outcome-level view of how prefix accumulation affects teacher recovery. English translations are shown in gray. Figure 7: Qualitative comparison on medium-resource Thai problem. The base model uses an incorrect asymmetric parameter range, while COPSD reports only an incomplete enumeration of five solutions. TOPSD factorizes the equation as (4x 3y)(3x + 2y) = 0, counts both parameterized solution families over their complete ranges, and obtains the correct answer 117. English translations are shown in gray. Figure 8: Qualitative comparison on low-resource Telugu problem. The base model forms an incorrect determinant-area expression, and COPSD produces repetitive reasoning without valid area derivation or boxed answer. TOPSD correctly derives the triangle area as 1012(i + j), computes S(n) = 1012n(n + 1)2, and obtains the correct limiting value 1012. English translations are shown in gray.
